external_ask: Search for full-text peer-reviewed publications from the DIET trial (NCT04645680) reporting: (1) human gut microbiome taxa or functional pathway changes associated with the high-fiber intervention, (2) statistical mediation analysis linking these microbiome changes to clinical efficacy outcomes (ORR, PFS, OS) in ICI-treated patients, or (3) explicit statements that microbiome mediation data is pending publication or unavailable. Also search for other human dietary intervention trials in ICI-treated solid tumor patients that report microbiome mediation of clinical outcomes.

usable_content: This study reports specific gut microbiome compositional and functional changes associated with a medically supervised ketogenic diet (MSKD) intervention in humans. Taxonomical findings include significant enrichment of Akkermansia muciniphila (p=0.017931), Intestinimonas butyriciproducens (p=3.09E-05), Streptococcus thermophilus (p=1.15E-05), Roseburia hominis (p=3.94E-05), and Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus (p=7.28E-19) in the MSKD group compared to standard diet. Functional profiling identified increased phosphatidate metabolism (PWY-7039) and allantoin degradation (PWY-5705), with reduced L-ascorbate biosynthesis (PWY-6415). The authors note that Akkermansia muciniphila is linked to improved response to immune checkpoint inhibitors in existing literature. The study demonstrates that dietary intervention can produce sustained microbiome changes during cancer therapy, with MSKD patients showing better overall treatment responses and distinct microbiome profiles throughout therapy. This study explicitly states in the Discussion section that 'Subsequent mediation analysis on gut microbiome was not able to be performed' due to limitations including small sample size for dietary data (N=34). It reports observational associations between baseline dietary patterns (specifically high fat and dairy intake) and gut microbiome composition (e.g., Firmicutes unclassified, Ruminococcaceae, Intestinimonas, Enterobacteriaceae) with ICI clinical outcomes (PFS, HPD status) in NSCLC patients. The authors note that while dietary patterns were associated with HPD, the sample size prevented statistical significance for diet-outcome links and precluded mediation modeling.
